section: Step 5.2: Mean isoscape and uncertainty in a single pass
text:
Step 5.2: Mean isoscape and uncertainty in a single pass
A random forest gives one prediction per pixel (the mean of all trees). A quantile random forest can also predict quantiles of the distribution in each pixel. The 15.9% and 84.1% quantiles bracket 68% of the predictions (±1 SD if the distribution is normal). Half of this range is our uncertainty (1 SD), which is what we need for Bayesian assignment with assignR in Module 3.
terra::predict() reads the rasters block by block (so memory is not a problem), calls our small function on each block, and writes the three layers (mean, Q15.9, Q84.1) directly to a GeoTIFF.






This step takes a few minutes



If memory is limited, increase steps. If it is too slow, the results are already in Output/rf_all_pred.tif and Output/rf_all_sd.tif.



# For a block of pixels: mean prediction + 15.9% and 84.1% quantiles
predict_mean_quantiles <- function(model, data, ...) {
  q <- predict(model, data = data, type = "quantiles", quantiles = c(0.159, 0.841))$predictions
  cbind(mean = predict(model, data = data)$predictions, q159 = q[, 1], q841 = q[, 2])
}

rf_pred <- terra::predict(stack_sel, RF_all$finalModel, fun = predict_mean_quantiles, na.rm = TRUE,
                          filename = "Output/rf_all_pred_quantiles1.tif", overwrite = TRUE,
                          wopt = list(steps = 20, names = c("mean", "q159", "q841")))

# Mean isoscape and uncertainty (1 SD = half of the 68% interval)
rf_sr    <- rf_pred[["mean"]]
rf_sr_sd <- (rf_pred[["q841"]] - rf_pred[["q159"]]) / 2

writeRaster(rf_sr,    filename = "Output/rf_all_pred.tif", overwrite = TRUE)
writeRaster(rf_sr_sd, filename = "Output/rf_all_sd.tif",   overwrite = TRUE)

Think · Pair · Share: patterns and uncertainty
Mean isoscape and 1 SD from the quantile random forest. Can you explain the patterns, and would you trust this map to assign a butterfly?


💭 Think 2 min

plot(c(rf_sr, rf_sr_sd))

On your own:

Where is the predicted ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr highest and lowest?
Where is the SD highest and lowest?



🤝 Pair 3 min
With your neighbour:

Explain the patterns with geology and Sr sources.
Is the SD high where there are no data, where the geology is complex, or both?
Do you see artefacts: straight edges, blocks, smooth coordinate-like gradients?



📣 Share 3 min
Tell the room:

Where would you trust this map for assignment in Module 3?
Where would you sample next?










Things you might have noticed





🪨 Spatial patterns

Radiogenic highs (> 0.74) in the north-east and along the Orange River and Namaqualand: old granites and gneisses of the Kaapvaal Craton and the Namaqua-Natal belt.
Lows (< 0.712) over Lesotho: the Drakensberg (Karoo) flood basalts.
Low values along the coast from sea-salt Sr. In the south-western Cape, a mosaic of Cape Granite Suite, Table Mountain Group, Malmesbury Group and Quaternary sands.

📊 Uncertainty

The highest SD (> 0.02) is over the same radiogenic terrains: old rocks have very heterogeneous minerals, and there are few sites.
The SD is low over the Karoo interior despite sparse data. A quantile random forest reports the spread of similar training sites, not the distance to the data.
So the SD can underestimate the error where the model extrapolates. Pair it with an area of applicability (Meyer & Pebesma 2021, CAST::aoa()).
Check sharp boundaries and blocky shapes against the covariates that created them. For example, the straight north–south edges in the south-western Cape SD map follow no geological contact: they likely come from the coarse (~1–2°) deposition layers that entered the model with candidate_set <- "all".

🦋 For assignment

The SD map becomes the isoscape uncertainty in assignR::pdRaster(). An SD that is too small gives over-confident assignments.
Sample next where the SD is high or the model extrapolates (north-east, Northern Cape, interior).

Take-home: an isoscape is a mean and an uncertainty, and the assignment inherits both.

title: 4. Predictor selection and cross-validation
text:
Step 4.1: Training set
If Sections 1 to 3 took too long, you can start here: the training set is saved in Output/.

sr_agg <- read.table("Output/sr_agg_all.txt", sep = "\t", h = T)

# Training sites as sf points (Eckert IV), used for maps and distances below
sites_sf <- st_as_sf(sr_agg, coords = c("X", "Y"), crs = eck4, remove = FALSE)

# Small helper used throughout Step 4: cross-validated predictions of a ranger
# model for a set of predictors and a vector of fold numbers (one per site).
# It returns RMSE and R2 of the out-of-fold predictions.
cv_ranger <- function(vars, folds, data = sr_agg, num.trees = 300) {
  pred <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(data))
  for (k in unique(folds)) {
    test <- folds == k
    m <- ranger(x = data[!test, vars, drop = FALSE], y = data$X87Sr86Sr[!test],
                num.trees = num.trees, seed = 1)
    pred[test] <- predict(m, data[test, vars, drop = FALSE])$predictions
  }
  c(RMSE = sqrt(mean((data$X87Sr86Sr - pred)^2)), R2 = cor(data$X87Sr86Sr, pred)^2)
}

title: 4. Predictor selection and cross-validation
text:
Step 4.2: Random vs. spatial cross-validation
In a regular (random) k-fold cross-validation, the sites are split at random into 10 folds, and each fold is predicted by a model trained on the other 9. But ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr data are spatially clustered: in South Africa, most sites are in the south-western Cape. A test site almost always has a training site a few hundred metres away, with the same geology and the same ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr. Random cross-validation therefore measures how well the model interpolates between nearby sites, not how well it predicts the large unsampled regions of the map.
In a spatial-block cross-validation, the folds are geographical clusters of sites (here 10 clusters made with k-means on the X/Y coordinates). The model is always tested on a region it has not seen.






How are the blocks made? We choose the number of blocks (centers = 10); k-means then groups the sites into 10 geographical clusters, so the size of each block simply follows how the sites are clustered. k-means starts from random centres, but nstart = 20 keeps the best of 20 starts and set.seed(1) makes the result reproducible. The block size is not estimated or optimised: we only check afterwards (Fig. S5) that the spatial CV distances look like the map’s. Methods such as kNNDM (CAST::knndm(), Linnenbrink et al. 2024) go further and build the folds so that the two distance distributions match.




# Random folds (10-fold)
set.seed(1)
random_folds <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = nrow(sr_agg)))

# Spatial folds: 10 geographical clusters of sites (k-means on the coordinates)
# (more advanced alternatives: blockCV package, or CAST::knndm, Linnenbrink et al., 2024)
set.seed(1)
spatial_folds <- kmeans(sr_agg[, c("X", "Y")], centers = 10, nstart = 20)$cluster

# Map of the two fold designs
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0))
plot(st_geometry(za_p), main = "Random 10-fold CV", border = "grey50")
points(sr_agg$X, sr_agg$Y, col = rainbow(10)[random_folds], pch = 16, cex = 0.6)
plot(st_geometry(za_p), main = "Spatial-block 10-fold CV", border = "grey50")
points(sr_agg$X, sr_agg$Y, col = rainbow(10)[spatial_folds], pch = 16, cex = 0.6)




Output of Step 4.2: random folds are mixed everywhere; spatial folds are blocks


The spatial blocks are very unequal: the smallest holds 5 sites and the largest 112.






📖 How to read the fold maps





Each dot is a training site, coloured by the fold it belongs to.

Random CV (left): the colours are mixed everywhere. When one fold is left out for testing, every test site still has neighbours of other colours (in the training set) a few hundred metres away.
Spatial CV (right): each colour is a geographical block. When a block is left out, the model must predict a whole region it has never seen, just like the unsampled parts of the map.




A good cross-validation should mimic the prediction situation (Meyer & Pebesma, 2022). We compare the distance from each test site to its nearest training site with the distance from each pixel of the map to its nearest training site.


Show the code
# Distance (km) from each point of 'from' to its nearest point in 'to'
nn_dist <- function(from, to) {
  idx <- st_nearest_feature(from, to)
  as.numeric(st_distance(from, to[idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 1000
}

# 1. Prediction situation: 5000 random pixels of the map -> nearest training site
map_pts <- st_as_sf(spatSample(r.srsrq1, size = 5000, method = "random", na.rm = TRUE, as.points = TRUE))
map_pts <- suppressWarnings(st_set_crs(map_pts, st_crs(sites_sf)))   # same Eckert IV projection, harmonise the CRS label
d_map <- nn_dist(map_pts, sites_sf)

# 2. Cross-validation situation: each test site -> nearest training site of the other folds
cv_dist <- function(folds) {
  unlist(lapply(unique(folds), function(k) nn_dist(sites_sf[folds == k, ], sites_sf[folds != k, ])))
}
d_random  <- cv_dist(random_folds)
d_spatial <- cv_dist(spatial_folds)

dist_df <- rbind(data.frame(type = "Map pixels -> training sites (prediction)", dist = d_map),
                 data.frame(type = "Random CV: test -> training sites", dist = d_random),
                 data.frame(type = "Spatial CV: test -> training sites", dist = d_spatial))

p_dist <- ggplot(dist_df, aes(x = dist + 0.1, colour = type, fill = type)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000), labels = c("0", "1", "10", "100", "1000")) +
  labs(x = "Distance to nearest training site (km, log scale)", y = "Density", colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.direction = "vertical")
p_dist
ggsave("Output/FigS5_distances_CV.pdf", p_dist, width = 8, height = 6)

# Median distances (km)
round(c(map = median(d_map), random_CV = median(d_random), spatial_CV = median(d_spatial)), 1)





Output of Step 4.2 (Fig. S5): distance to the nearest training site for map pixels, random CV and spatial CV


What you should see:
##        map  random_CV spatial_CV
##       83.8        5.5       80.5






📖 How to read Fig. S5





Each curve is the distribution of a distance to the nearest training site (log scale: 1, 10, 100 km).

Red, map pixels → training sites: the prediction situation. Most pixels of South Africa are 30–300 km from any data.
Green, random CV: the test sites are 0.1–30 km from training data, far closer than the map pixels. Random CV tests an easier problem than the one we actually face.
Blue, spatial CV: the curve overlaps the red one. Spatial CV tests the model at the distances where it will be used.

What to look for: the CV curve that matches the red one gives the most honest error estimate.









🔍 Look carefully



In random cross-validation, the test sites are typically a few km from a training site (median ~6 km), whereas the median map pixel is ~84 km from any data. The spatial cross-validation (~81 km) is much closer to the real prediction situation. This is why we use the spatial cross-validation for predictor selection (Step 4.4) and tuning (Step 4.6).

title: 4. Predictor selection and cross-validation
text:
Step 4.3: Predictor selection with VSURF
VSURF (Variable Selection Using Random Forests) ranks the predictors by their importance in a series of random forests, then removes the less important ones step by step. It returns three nested sets:








Set
VSURF step
What it keeps




varselect.thres
thresholding
removes the variables indistinguishable from noise; keeps most variables


varselect.interp
interpretation
all the variables related to ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr, including correlated ones


varselect.pred
prediction
the smallest set that gives the best prediction; very restrictive



Here we use varselect.interp by default: it keeps more variables (and therefore more processes) for nearly the same accuracy. Then, in Step 4.4, we prune it with the spatial cross-validation.






VSURF behaves like a random cross-validation



VSURF uses the out-of-bag error, which does not know about spatial autocorrelation. Interpret its results cautiously.








This step takes ~8 minutes



Start it before lunch! If your laptop is slow, load the pre-computed result instead: load("Output/VSURF_all.gz") (note the .gz), then continue with the next chunk.



# Set a random seed for reproducibility
set.seed(1)
# Create a copy of 'sr_agg'
sr_agg0 <- sr_agg

# Apply VSURF algorithm to select relevant variables for predicting 'X87Sr86Sr'
# Using the 'ranger' implementation with parallelization
# Columns 1 to 3 are X87Sr86Sr, X and Y: the covariates start at column 4
sr_agg1.vsurf <- VSURF(
  sr_agg0[, 4:ncol(sr_agg0)],
  sr_agg0$X87Sr86Sr,
  mtry = max(floor((ncol(sr_agg0) - 3)/3), 1),
 ntree.thres = 1000,
 nfor.thres = 20,
 nmin = 1,
 ntree.interp = 1000,
 nfor.interp = 10,
 nsd = 1,
 ntree.pred = 1000,
 nfor.pred = 10,
 nmj = 1,
  RFimplem = "ranger",
  parallel = TRUE,
  ncores = n_cores,
  clusterType = "PSOCK"
)

save(sr_agg1.vsurf, file = "Output/VSURF_all")


#Plot VSURF results
plot(sr_agg1.vsurf)

# Names of the covariates (columns 4 to end)
covariate_names <- names(sr_agg0)[4:ncol(sr_agg0)]

# Variables selected at each of the three VSURF steps
vsurf_sets <- list(thres  = covariate_names[sr_agg1.vsurf$varselect.thres],
                   interp = covariate_names[sr_agg1.vsurf$varselect.interp],
                   pred   = covariate_names[sr_agg1.vsurf$varselect.pred])
lengths(vsurf_sets)
vsurf_sets

# Choose the VSURF step used for the next steps: "interp" (default) or "pred" (as in the global script)
vsurf_step <- "interp"
vars_vsurf <- vsurf_sets[[vsurf_step]]




Output of Step 4.3: the four VSURF panels








📖 How to read the VSURF plot





VSURF draws four panels, one per step. On every x-axis, the variables are sorted from most to least important.








Panel
What it shows
What to look for in our run




Top left: VI mean
Mean variable importance (VI) of each of the 42 covariates, over 20 random forests. The red line is the noise threshold.
Importance drops very fast: a handful of covariates carry most of the signal. Variables below the red line are dropped (here only 1, so 41 are kept: thres).


Top right: VI standard deviation
How much the importance of each variable varies between the forests. VSURF fits a tree (green) to this curve to set the noise threshold (red dashed line).
The importance of the top variables is stable; the tail is noisy.


Bottom left: nested models
OOB error of random forests built with the top 1, 2, 3… variables. The red vertical line marks the interpretation set: the smallest model whose error is within 1 SD of the minimum.
The error falls steeply over the first ~5 variables, then is almost flat. The red line is at 16 variables (interp).


Bottom right: predictive models
OOB error as variables are added one by one, keeping a variable only if it lowers the error enough.
Only 9 variables survive (pred), for about the same error.



Units: the OOB error is a mean squared error in (⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr)². An error of 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ is an RMSE of √(1.5 × 10⁻⁵) ≈ 0.0039, very close to the random CV RMSE (0.0039 in Step 4.6). That is no coincidence: the OOB error is a kind of random cross-validation, so it is just as optimistic.
Interpretation vs. prediction set: the 16 interp variables include correlated “twins” (e.g. r.srsrq1, .f05 and .f25) and the coarse layers (r.salt, r.dust, r.volc, r.foss). The 9 pred variables are fewer but still include the three bedrock layers and r.salt: VSURF removes variables that don’t lower the OOB error, not variables that are correlated.

title: 4. Predictor selection and cross-validation
section: Step 4.4: Spatial pruning of the predictors
text:
Step 4.4: Spatial pruning of the predictors
Some predictors help to “recognise” the places where the training sites are (they act as a proxy for coordinates) but do not help to predict unsampled regions. To find them, we do a backward elimination with the spatial cross-validation:

Compute the spatial-CV RMSE with all the VSURF variables.
Remove each variable in turn and recompute the spatial-CV RMSE.
If removing one variable improves the RMSE by more than tol (2%), remove the one that improves it most and go back to 2. Otherwise stop.

Why 2%? The spatial-CV RMSE changes by ~0.5–1% just by changing the random seed, so smaller “improvements” are noise. (For a more systematic approach, see the forward feature selection with spatial CV of Meyer et al. 2018, in the CAST package.)

spatial_pruning <- TRUE
tol <- 0.02
ntree_pruning <- 1000

vars_final <- vars_vsurf
best <- cv_ranger(vars_final, spatial_folds, num.trees = ntree_pruning)["RMSE"]
pruning_path <- data.frame(step = 0, n_vars = length(vars_final), RMSE = best, removed = "start (VSURF set)")

if (spatial_pruning) {
  repeat {
    if (length(vars_final) <= 2) break
    # spatial-CV RMSE after removing each variable in turn
    rmse_without <- sapply(vars_final, function(v) cv_ranger(setdiff(vars_final, v), spatial_folds, num.trees = ntree_pruning)["RMSE"])
    if (min(rmse_without) < best * (1 - tol)) {
      worst <- vars_final[which.min(rmse_without)]
      vars_final <- setdiff(vars_final, worst)
      best <- min(rmse_without)
      pruning_path <- rbind(pruning_path, data.frame(step = nrow(pruning_path), n_vars = length(vars_final),
                                                     RMSE = best, removed = worst))
    } else break
  }
}
pruning_path
vars_final

# Training dataset for random forest: 87Sr/86Sr + selected predictors
training_rf <- sr_agg[, c("X87Sr86Sr", vars_final)]

In our run, removing any single variable never improved the spatial-CV RMSE by more than 2%, so the spatial pruning kept all 16 VSURF variables.






📖 How to read the pruning output





pruning_path has one row per step: the number of variables, the spatial-CV RMSE and the variable removed. Here it has a single row (“start (VSURF set)”): no removal helped by more than the 2% tolerance, which is why the script does not draw the pruning plot. Try a smaller tol in Exercise 2 to see variables being removed.

title: 4. Predictor selection and cross-validation
text:
Step 4.5: Compare the predictor sets
For each set of predictors, we compare the R² obtained with random and with spatial cross-validation.


Show the code
sets <- list("All candidates" = names(sr_agg)[4:ncol(sr_agg)],
             "VSURF thres" = vsurf_sets$thres,
             "VSURF interp" = vsurf_sets$interp,
             "VSURF pred" = vsurf_sets$pred,
             "Final (spatially pruned)" = vars_final)

set_compare <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(sets), function(s) {
  data.frame(set = s, n_vars = length(sets[[s]]),
             CV = c("Random CV", "Spatial CV"),
             R2 = c(cv_ranger(sets[[s]], random_folds)["R2"], cv_ranger(sets[[s]], spatial_folds)["R2"]))
}))
set_compare$set <- factor(paste0(set_compare$set, "\n(", set_compare$n_vars, " var.)"),
                          levels = unique(paste0(set_compare$set, "\n(", set_compare$n_vars, " var.)")))
set_compare

p_sets <- ggplot(set_compare, aes(x = set, y = R2, fill = CV)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(R2, 2)), position = position_dodge(0.9), vjust = -0.3, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Random CV" = "grey60", "Spatial CV" = "darkorange")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Cross-validated R2", fill = NULL, title = "Random CV hides what spatial CV reveals") +
  theme_minimal()
p_sets
ggsave("Output/FigS6_predictor_sets_CV.pdf", p_sets, width = 10, height = 5)

# Path of the spatial pruning
if (nrow(pruning_path) > 1) {
  ggplot(pruning_path, aes(x = step, y = RMSE)) +
    geom_line() + geom_point() +
    geom_text(aes(label = removed), vjust = -0.8, size = 3) +
    labs(x = "Pruning step", y = "Spatial-CV RMSE", title = "Spatial pruning of the VSURF variables") +
    theme_minimal()
}





Output of Step 4.5 (Fig. S6): random CV barely changes between predictor sets (0.75–0.79); spatial CV separates them (0.54–0.70)








📖 How to read Fig. S6





Each pair of bars is one predictor set (number of variables below): grey = random CV R², orange = spatial CV R².

Grey bars are all alike (0.75–0.79): random CV cannot tell the sets apart.
Orange bars differ a lot (0.54–0.70): with all 42 candidates or the 41 thres variables, the spatial R² is low. Many weak or coordinate-like variables help the model recognise places, not processes.
The gap between grey and orange is the optimism of random CV. It is largest for the sets with the most variables.
pred (9 variables) has the best spatial R² (0.70): fewer, less redundant predictors transfer better to new regions. Our final set (16 variables, 0.66) keeps more processes for interpretation, at a small cost.

title: 4. Predictor selection and cross-validation
section: Step 4.6: Tune and train the random forest
text:
Step 4.6: Tune and train the random forest

We use the fast ranger implementation, which uses all the cores of your computer by itself.
We tune mtry (number of variables sampled at each split) and min.node.size (minimum number of sites in a terminal node).
The tuning uses the spatial folds: we choose the hyperparameters that predict new regions best.
The model is trained with quantreg = TRUE (quantile regression forest, Meinshausen 2006). The same model gives the mean isoscape and its uncertainty in Section 6.


# Spatial-block cross-validation: one spatial cluster is left out at a time
# index    = for each fold, the rows used for training (all the other blocks)
# indexOut = for each fold, the rows used for testing (the block left out)
blocks <- sort(unique(spatial_folds))
fitControl_spatial <- trainControl(
   method = "cv",
   index    = lapply(blocks, function(k) which(spatial_folds != k)),
   indexOut = lapply(blocks, function(k) which(spatial_folds == k)),
   savePredictions = "final",
   verboseIter = FALSE,
   allowParallel = FALSE)   # ranger is already multi-threaded

# Tuning grid: mtry and min.node.size (splitrule fixed to "variance" for regression)
n_pred <- length(vars_final)
tunegrid <- expand.grid(mtry = unique(pmax(1, round(n_pred * c(0.2, 0.33, 0.5, 0.75)))),
                        splitrule = "variance",
                        min.node.size = c(5, 10, 20))

set.seed(1)
RF_all <- train(X87Sr86Sr ~ ., data = training_rf,
                method = "ranger", metric = "RMSE",
                tuneGrid = tunegrid, trControl = fitControl_spatial,
                num.trees = 500, quantreg = TRUE, importance = "permutation", seed = 1)

save(RF_all, file = "Output/RF_all")

# Note: in this table, Rsquared is the mean of the R2 computed within each spatial
# block. It is low because each block covers a small range of 87Sr/86Sr. The
# tuning uses RMSE; the pooled R2 of all out-of-block predictions is computed below.
# The spatial blocks have different sizes (one contains most of the Cape sites).
RF_all
RF_all$bestTune

What you should see (part of the output):
##   mtry min.node.size    RMSE Rsquared
##      3             5 0.00520    0.389
##      5             5 0.00489    0.406
##      8            10 0.00470    0.316   <- best (lowest RMSE)
##     12             5 0.00473    0.329






📖 How to read the tuning output





Each row is one combination of hyperparameters, evaluated on the 10 spatial blocks.

mtry: how many variables each split can choose from. Small values make trees more different from each other; large values let every tree use the strongest variable.
min.node.size: the minimum number of sites in a final leaf. Larger values give smoother predictions.
RMSE is the mean over the 10 blocks, and caret picks the lowest: mtry = 8, min.node.size = 10. The differences are small (0.0047–0.0054), so the model is not very sensitive to these settings.
Rsquared here is low (0.3–0.4) because it is computed within each block, and each block covers a narrow range of ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr. Don’t compare it with the pooled R² below.




For comparison, the classic random repeated 10-fold cross-validation with the same hyperparameters:

# Classic random repeated 10-fold cross-validation with the same hyperparameters (for comparison)
fitControl_random <- trainControl(
   method = "repeatedcv",  # 10-fold Crossvalidation
   number = 10,
   repeats = 5,            # Repeated five times
   savePredictions = "final",
   allowParallel = FALSE)

set.seed(1)
RF_random <- train(X87Sr86Sr ~ ., data = training_rf,
                   method = "ranger", metric = "RMSE",
                   tuneGrid = RF_all$bestTune, trControl = fitControl_random,
                   num.trees = 500, seed = 1)

cv_compare <- rbind(
  Random_CV  = postResample(RF_random$pred$pred, RF_random$pred$obs),
  Spatial_CV = postResample(RF_all$pred$pred, RF_all$pred$obs))
cv_compare
write.csv(cv_compare, "Output/cross_validation_random_vs_spatial.csv")

What you should see:
##                   RMSE  Rsquared         MAE
## Random_CV  0.003947601 0.7706560 0.002069309
## Spatial_CV 0.004834838 0.6633814 0.002958629

title: 4. Predictor selection and cross-validation
text:
Step 4.7: Plot the cross-validation results


Show the plotting code
cv_pred <- rbind(data.frame(RF_random$pred[, c("obs", "pred")], CV = "Random 10-fold CV (repeated 5 times)"),
                 data.frame(RF_all$pred[, c("obs", "pred")],    CV = "Spatial-block 10-fold CV"))

# Axis limits adapted to the South African 87Sr/86Sr range
sr_lim <- range(c(cv_pred$obs, cv_pred$pred))

p1 <- ggplot(cv_pred, aes(x = obs, y = pred)) +
    geom_bin_2d(binwidth = 0.001) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = 3) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "black") +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, trans = "sqrt") +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = sr_lim, ylim = sr_lim) +
    facet_wrap(~ CV) +
    labs(fill = "Count") +
    xlab("87Sr/86Srobs") +
    ylab("87Sr/86Srmod")

p2 <- ggplot(cv_pred, aes(x = obs, y = pred - obs)) +
    geom_bin_2d(binwidth = 0.001, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, trans = "sqrt") +
    facet_wrap(~ CV) +
    xlab("87Sr/86Srobs") +
    ylab("Residuals")

p3 <- p1 / p2 + plot_annotation(
    title = "Model performance: random vs. spatial cross-validation"
  )
p3
ggsave("Output/FigS2.pdf", p3, width = 14, height = 12)





Output of Step 4.7 (Fig. S2): same model, same data: R² = 0.77 with random CV, 0.66 with spatial CV








📖 How to read Fig. S2






Top row, observed vs. predicted: each cell counts sites (darker = more). The dotted line is the 1:1 line (a perfect model); the black line is the regression through the points.
The black line is flatter than 1:1 in both panels: high values are under-predicted, and the lowest values are slightly over-predicted. Radiogenic sites (> 0.73) are rare, so the model pulls them towards the mean. This is typical of random forests, which average many trees.
The spatial panel is more scattered and flatter than the random one: predicting a region the model has never seen is harder.
Bottom row, residuals (predicted − observed): a cloud centred on 0 with no trend would be ideal. The downward trend at high observed values is the same under-prediction of radiogenic sites.




Where are the large errors of the spatial cross-validation?


Show the code
# Map of the spatial-CV residuals (observed - predicted) at each site
res_sp <- RF_all$pred[order(RF_all$pred$rowIndex), ]
sites_sf$resid_spatial <- res_sp$obs - res_sp$pred

p_res <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = za_p, fill = "grey95", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_sf(data = sites_sf[order(abs(sites_sf$resid_spatial)), ], aes(colour = resid_spatial), size = 1.5) +
  scale_colour_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "grey90", high = "red", midpoint = 0,
                         limits = c(-0.015, 0.015), oob = scales::squish, name = "obs - pred") +
  coord_sf(xlim = range(sr_agg$X) + c(-1e5, 1e5), ylim = range(sr_agg$Y) + c(-1e5, 1e5)) +
  ggtitle("Spatial-CV residuals") +
  theme_minimal()
p_res
ggsave("Output/FigS7_residual_map.pdf", p_res, width = 8, height = 7)





Output of Step 4.7 (Fig. S7): spatial-CV residuals (observed − predicted) at each site








📖 How to read Fig. S7





Each dot is a site, coloured by its spatial-CV residual (observed − predicted): red = the model predicts too low, blue = too high, pale = good.

The errors cluster in space: under-predicted (red) sites group in the north-east (around the Bushveld) and in KwaZulu-Natal; over-predicted (blue) sites group on parts of the west coast.
Clustered residuals mean the model misses a regional process, for example an old radiogenic basement or a local dust source that no covariate describes well. They are also a sign of spatial autocorrelation, which is why random CV is optimistic.
What would you do? Look for a covariate that explains the pattern, or collect more data in those regions.





Think · Pair · Share: random vs. spatial CV
Same model, same data: random CV R² = 0.77 (RMSE 0.0039), spatial-block CV R² = 0.66 (RMSE 0.0048). Which one would you report in a paper, and why?


💭 Think 1 min

cv_compare

On your own, compare the fold maps and the distance plot: test sites sit ~6 km (random) vs. ~81 km (spatial) from the training data, and map pixels sit ~84 km away.


🤝 Pair 3 min
With your neighbour:

Random CV barely changes between predictor sets (0.75–0.79); spatial CV separates them (0.54–0.70). What does that tell you about OOB error and VSURF?
What are the weaknesses of spatial CV?



📣 Share 5 min
Tell the room:

When would random CV be acceptable?
How would you design spatial folds for your own study area and sampling design?










Things you might have noticed





🎲 Problems with random CV

Test sites sit next to training sites: it measures interpolation, not prediction in unsampled regions.
It is over-optimistic, and it rewards covariates that act as coordinates (the coarse aerosol layers).
It cannot tell a good predictor set from a bad one, and the OOB error and VSURF share this blind spot.

🧩 Problems with spatial CV

Results depend on the number and size of the blocks (Exercise 3). k-means blocks are unequal: one holds most of the Cape sites.
It can be pessimistic if the blocks force more extrapolation than the map needs.
Within-block R² is low because each block spans a narrow Sr range: pool the predictions (as in Step 4.7).

✅ When random CV is OK

Dense, even sampling, where map pixels are as close to the data as the test sites are.
The goal is interpolation inside the sampled area.

📐 Designing your folds

Match the CV distance distribution to the prediction distances (Meyer & Pebesma 2022; CAST::knndm(), the blockCV package).
Use the same CV for predictor selection, tuning and reporting, and show the residual map.
Both CVs under-predict the radiogenic sites (> 0.73).

Take-home: report the spatial CV. It is the honest estimate for the places your animals actually came from.

How many variables are kept?

In our run, the prediction step keeps 9 variables, and its spatial R² (0.70) is higher than with the 16 interpretation variables (0.66) (Fig. S6). Fewer, less redundant predictors can transfer better to new regions. Which of the coarse layers survive?

How many variables are kept?
How does the spatial CV change?









Hint

Exercise 3: spatial folds






🧩 Your turn



Change the number of spatial clusters (centers = 10 in Step 4.2) to 5 or 20.

How do the distance distributions change?

Things to look for





Fewer, larger blocks push the test sites further from the training data, so the spatial R² usually drops. More, smaller blocks bring the CV distances closer to the random CV. The best design is the one whose distances look most like the map’s.

text:
Summary






Key takeaways




Random CV measures interpolation between nearby sites; spatial CV measures prediction in new regions.
OOB error and VSURF behave like random CV, so we prune and tune with spatial CV.
The final model keeps 16 predictors, with R² = 0.66 in spatial CV (0.77 in random CV).

title: Extra: your own study area
text:
In this section




You’ll learn: how to adapt this workflow to build an isoscape for your own study area
You’ll need: the global covariate rasters from OSF and screened bioavailable ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr data for your area
Time: read it after the workshop

title: Extra: your own study area
text:
Overview
The rasters in Project_Raster/clipped_za are the global covariates, already clipped to South Africa. To build an isoscape somewhere else, go back to the global rasters and clip them to your own area. The rest of the script stays the same.

title: Extra: your own study area
text:
1. Download the global rasters
Download the global covariates (Eckert IV, 1 km) from the Projected_rasters folder of the OSF project, and put them all in one folder, e.g. Global_rasters/ next to Data/ and Project_Raster/. They are already in the same projection and resolution and snapped to the same grid, so all you need to do is clip them.






Large files



The global 1 km rasters are much larger than the South African ones. Download only the layers you need, and keep enough free disk space for the clipped copies.

title: Extra: your own study area
section: 2. Clip them to your study area
text:
2. Clip them to your study area
Define your study area as a polygon, reproject it to Eckert IV, add a buffer, then crop and mask every raster.

library(terra)
library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)

eck4 <- "+proj=eck4 +lon_0=0 +x_0=0 +y_0=0 +ellps=WGS84 +units=m +no_defs"

global_dir <- "Global_rasters"                  # folder with the global OSF rasters
out_dir    <- "Project_Raster/clipped_myarea"   # where the clipped rasters will go
dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Study area: here one or more countries from Natural Earth...
area <- ne_countries(country = c("Kenya", "Tanzania"), scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf")
# ...or your own polygon: area <- st_read("my_study_area.shp")

area <- area |>
  st_transform(eck4) |>
  st_union() |>
  st_buffer(50000)   # 50 km buffer (see the tip below)
area_v <- vect(area)

# Crop and mask every global raster to the study area
for (f in list.files(global_dir, pattern = "\\.tif$", full.names = TRUE)) {
  r <- rast(f)
  r <- crop(r, project(area_v, crs(r)), mask = TRUE)
  writeRaster(r, file.path(out_dir, basename(f)), overwrite = TRUE)
}
list.files(out_dir)







Why a buffer?



The neighbourhood covariates (Step 2.8) average the geology within 25 km. Near the edge of a tightly clipped area, those windows are cut in half. A buffer of at least 25 km (here 50 km) keeps them complete. It also lets you use training sites just outside your area of interest.

title: Extra: your own study area
section: 3. Point the script to your rasters
text:
3. Point the script to your rasters
In the setup chunk, change the raster folder:

raster_dir <- "Project_Raster/clipped_myarea"

Then delete or rename Project_Raster/neighbourhood/, so that the neighbourhood layers (Step 2.8) are recomputed for your area instead of re-using the South African ones.

title: Extra: your own study area
text:
4. Adjust the list of covariates
On the Covariates page, Steps 2.2 to 2.7 load each raster by name, and Step 2.9 lists them in predictor_names. Every name in that list must exist in your folder.

Remove the South African layers: r.geomap and r.vegmap exist only for South Africa. The iSDA soil layers (r.africa.*) cover Africa only: outside Africa, remove them too.
Check the other layers: a few layers in the South African set are not part of the global script (r.pet_clim, r.pfert, r.biofuels, r.biogenic). Keep them only if you have them.
Add your own regional layers if they exist (detailed geological maps, radiometric surveys, soil geochemistry…). They must be in Eckert IV at 1 km, on the same grid. project(my_layer, r.srsrq1) does this for you.

Instead of editing Steps 2.2 to 2.7 one line at a time, you can load everything in the folder at once. Run this chunk in place of Steps 2.2 to 2.7:

files <- list.files(raster_dir, pattern = "\\.tif$", full.names = TRUE)
for (f in files) assign(sub("\\.tif$", "", basename(f)), rast(f))

Then run Step 2.8 (neighbourhood geology) as usual, and replace the predictor_names list in Step 2.9 with:

# Every raster in the folder is a candidate covariate, plus the neighbourhood layers of Step 2.8
predictor_names <- c(sub("\\.tif$", "", basename(files)), focal_names)

In the rest of Step 2.9, two lines refer to South African layers by name. Edit them if those layers are not in your folder:

for (p in c("r.geomap", "r.vegmap")) levels(stack_all[[p]]) <- NULL: delete it if you have no categorical maps (or put your own categorical layers in the list).
plot(stack_all[[c(..., "r.africa.Ca.0")]]): remove "r.africa.Ca.0" outside Africa.

title: Extra: your own study area
text:
5. Use your own training data
Replace Data/SouthAfrica_bioavailable_Sr_ARDUOUS.csv with screened bioavailable ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr data for your area, in the ARDUOUS format (see Module 1 and the ARDUOUS dataset). The script uses the columns collection_decimal_longitude, collection_decimal_latitude, 87Sr86Sr and material_type.

title: Extra: your own study area
text:
6. Re-think a few choices

Coarse layers (Step 3.5): inside one country, dust and sea-salt models are smooth gradients that act like coordinates. Over a continent, they vary for real and can be useful. Compare "all" and "no_coarse" with the spatial cross-validation.
Spatial folds (Step 4.2): choose the number of clusters to match your sampling design, and check that the cross-validation distances look like the map’s.
Time and memory: a larger area means more pixels. If the prediction (Step 5.2) runs out of memory, increase steps.
Few data in your area? A locally trained model needs enough sites to learn from. With very few data, a globally trained isoscape (Bataille et al. 2020) is often the better starting point.

title: Extra: your own study area
text:
Summary






Key takeaways




The South African rasters are the global covariates clipped to South Africa: you can clip the same global rasters to any area.
Add a buffer of at least 25 km, so the neighbourhood covariates are complete at the edges.
Remove the covariates that don’t exist in your area, add regional ones if you have them, and use your own screened training data.
With very few data, start from a globally trained isoscape.

title: 1. Training data
text:
Overview
This script is adapted from Bataille et al. (2020), “Advances in global bioavailable strontium isoscapes”. This version uses South Africa as a case study. Compared with the global version:

Training data: a harmonised and screened dataset of bioavailable ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr for South Africa in the ARDUOUS format, mostly from plants.
Covariates: the global Eckert IV 1 km rasters are already clipped to South Africa, so no cropping is needed and everything runs on a laptop.
New regional covariates: African soil chemistry (iSDA Africa), the 1:1M geological map of South Africa, the South African vegetation map, and neighbourhood (5, 10, 25 km) means of the bedrock ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr and geological age.
Spatial cross-validation: we compare random and spatial-block cross-validation, and use the spatial one to prune the predictors and tune the model.







More resources




Bataille, C. P., Crowley, B. E., Wooller, M. J., & Bowen, G. J. (2020). Advances in global bioavailable strontium isoscapes. Palaeogeography, Palaeoclimatology, Palaeoecology, 555, 109849. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.palaeo.2020.109849
Global predictor rasters: https://osf.io/a2r7g/

title: 1. Training data
text:
Step 1.1: Import the training data
The training dataset Data/SouthAfrica_bioavailable_Sr_ARDUOUS.csv has already been harmonised and screened for you, in the ARDUOUS format.






Not the Module 1 dataset



This is not the dataset screened in Module 1. It is a separate compilation for South Africa (SrBaseline, the Wang compilation and IsoBank), cleaned for this module. The screening steps are listed below.


This dataset mostly represents bioavailable ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr from plants (608 of 927 records, 66%), complemented by modern fauna with small home ranges (259 records, 28%: rodents, hyraxes, hares, snails, tortoises, small antelopes) and soil leachates (60 records, 6%). It includes 579 distinct sampling locations.






Screening applied






only records within South Africa, with coordinates and 0.700 < ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr < 0.800;
waters (rivers, groundwater) removed, because they integrate whole catchments;
humans, hominins, primates, elephants and ivory, domestic cattle, fish, birds, large and migratory herbivores and large carnivores removed, because their ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr does not reflect where they were collected;

Think · Pair · Share: a map for a butterfly
You want to find where painted ladies (Vanessa cardui) caught in South Africa grew up, from the ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr of their wings. What training data and what kind of bioavailable Sr map do you need?


💭 Think 2 min

table(sr_orig$material_type)

On your own, look at the sample types and the map above.

Where does a butterfly’s wing Sr come from?
When in its life is it fixed?



🤝 Pair 3 min
With your neighbour:

Which substrate is the best analogue for a butterfly: soils, plants or small-range fauna?
Which records would you keep or drop?
Is the spatial coverage good enough where your butterflies might come from?



📣 Share 3 min
Tell the room what map you would build:

All substrates or plants only?
Over what extent, at what resolution, and with what uncertainty?










Things you might have noticed





🌿 The best substrate

Wing Sr is fixed during the larval stage: caterpillars eat host-plant leaves, and adult wing chitin is not remodelled.
Herbaceous host plants (thistles, mallows, other Asteraceae) are the closest analogue: shallow roots, same Sr pool.
Soil leachates, deep-rooted trees and small mammals sample other Sr pools or larger areas, and can be offset from host plants.

🗺️ Is our dataset a good fit? Yes!

It is mostly plants (66%) plus small-range fauna (28%) that eat local plants, and everything that does not reflect local bioavailable Sr (waters, large or migratory animals, humans, fossils) has already been removed.
So it represents plant bioavailable Sr well. This is the isoscape we use for the butterflies in Module 3.
We also need an extent covering the whole potential natal range, ~1 km resolution (fine for a caterpillar), and a pixel-level uncertainty (SD) to feed assignR::pdRaster() in Module 3.

⚖️ Substrate vs. coverage

Substrate matters: always ask whether your training data sample the same Sr pool as your organism.
But bioavailable Sr data are still scarce. Removing every substrate that is not a perfect match would leave large regions with no data, and the isoscape would get worse, not better.
At this stage, more data and better coverage beat perfect substrate matching. The uncertainty (SD) map absorbs part of the substrate differences. Substrate-specific isoscapes will make sense once we have many more data.

⚠️ Watch out

579 sites, but most are in the south-western Cape: the interior (Karoo, Northern Cape, Limpopo) will be predicted from covariates, not data.

Take-home: think about substrate, but don’t screen your data to death. A well-screened, mostly plant dataset with good coverage is the right isoscape for a butterfly today.

title: 0. How random forest works
text:
In this section




You’ll learn: how a regression tree splits the data, why one tree is not enough, and how bagging and random forest fix it
You’ll need: nothing to run: this page has no code for RStudio
Time: about 15 minutes

title: 0. How random forest works
text:
Overview
In the talk, we saw that bioavailable ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr varies at many scales: continental terranes, regional bedrock, atmospheric gradients (dust, sea salt) and local sedimentary features. No single map captures all of them. A random forest learns how ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr relates to many maps at once (geology, climate, soils, atmospheric deposition…), and then predicts it everywhere.












✅ Why random forest for Sr?




Combines many geospatial layers seamlessly
Captures non-linear relationships and interactions
Can map multiscale patterns of bioavailable ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr
More accurate than interpolation or domain mapping











⚠️ Challenges




Needs a lot of training data
More computing than simpler methods
Harder to interpret: we need tools to look inside
Its uncertainty maps have limitations

title: 0. How random forest works
section: Step 0.1: A decision tree for regression
text:
Step 0.1: A decision tree for regression
A regression tree asks a series of yes/no questions about the covariates, and each answer sends a site down one branch. At the end of a branch (a leaf), the prediction is the mean ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr of the training sites that ended up there.


  
  
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
  
  
    yesno
    yesno
    yesno
  
  
    Age < 100 Myr?
    Coast < 10 km?
    Coast < 50 km?
    Age < 10 Myr?
    Coast < 100 km?
    Age < 300 Myr?
    Coast < 70 km?
  
  
    0.7090.710
    0.7110.712
    0.7110.713
    0.7150.720
  
  leaves: mean ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr of the training sites in each group

A toy regression tree: young rocks near the coast end up with low, seawater-like ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr; old rocks far inland with high, radiogenic values.

How does the tree choose its questions? At each node, the algorithm tries every covariate and every possible threshold, and keeps the split that makes the two groups as homogeneous as possible (the largest drop in the variance of ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr). It repeats this in each group until the groups are small.






Problems with a single tree




Overfitting: a deep tree ends up memorising the training sites, noise included.
Instability: add or remove a few sites and the whole tree can change.
Blocky predictions: a tree predicts one value per leaf, so a single-tree isoscape would be a patchwork of flat zones with sharp steps.
Greedy splits: each split is the best now, not necessarily the best for the whole tree.

title: 0. How random forest works
section: Step 0.2: Bagging, many trees on resampled data
text:
Step 0.2: Bagging, many trees on resampled data
Bagging (bootstrap aggregation) grows many trees, each on a different bootstrap sample of the sites: sites drawn at random with replacement, so each tree sees about two-thirds of them (some twice), and never sees the remaining third. The prediction is the average of all trees. Averaging cancels out much of the noise each tree has memorised.

title: 0. How random forest works
section: Step 0.3: Random forest, adding randomness to the splits
text:
Step 0.3: Random forest, adding randomness to the splits
A random forest is bagging plus one more trick: at each split, a tree may only choose among a random subset of the covariates (mtry of them). This stops every tree from starting with the same strong covariate, so the trees are more different from each other, and their average is more robust.


  
  
  Training sites
  579 sites × covariates
  
    
    
    
  
  
    in-bag~2/3
    OOB~1/3
    in-bag~2/3
    OOB~1/3
    in-bag~2/3
    OOB~1/3
    · · ·
  
  
    
    
    
  
  · · ·
  each split: best of mtry random covariates
  
  Prediction = average of all trees

Each tree grows on its own bootstrap sample and picks among a random subset of covariates at every split. The sites a tree never saw (out-of-bag, OOB) are used to test it.







💡 The out-of-bag (OOB) error



Each site is left out of about a third of the trees. Predicting each site with only the trees that never saw it gives a free estimate of the error, the OOB error, without a separate test set. VSURF uses it to rank the covariates (Step 4.3). But the OOB sites are scattered among the training sites, so the OOB error behaves like a random cross-validation: it is optimistic for spatial data (Step 4.2).

title: 0. How random forest works
0. How random forest works
section: Step 0.5: From a forest to an isoscape
text:
Step 0.5: From a forest to an isoscape
For an isoscape, each “site” is a training sample with its ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr and the values of ~60 covariates under it. Once the forest is trained, we give it the covariates of every 1 km pixel and it predicts ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr there.



The random forest isoscape workflow (Bataille et al. 2020): overlay the sites on the covariates, build the regression matrix, select and train the model, then predict every pixel


And the uncertainty? Each tree gives its own prediction for a pixel. A quantile random forest keeps the whole spread of training values in the leaves, not just their mean, so we can read the 15.9% and 84.1% quantiles and turn them into a standard deviation. That is our uncertainty map (Section 6).

text:
Summary






Key takeaways




A regression tree splits the sites with yes/no questions on the covariates; each leaf predicts the mean ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr of its sites.
One tree overfits and is unstable. Bagging averages many trees grown on bootstrap samples; random forest also randomises the covariates at each split.
The OOB error is a free error estimate, but it behaves like random cross-validation.
Random forests cannot extrapolate beyond their training data.

title: 2. Covariates
text:
Overview
We now load the covariates used to train the random forest. They describe the geological, environmental and climatic processes that control bioavailable ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr: the sources of Sr (bedrock, dust, sea salt), how it is mixed and weathered (soils, climate, sediments) and how it is taken up (vegetation).






Same projection, same grid



The rasters must share the same projection and resolution, and be snapped to each other. This preprocessing is slow for global layers, so it has been done for you: the global Eckert IV 1 km rasters (OSF) are already clipped to South Africa in Project_Raster/clipped_za.
Want to build an isoscape for your own study area? See the extra page Your own study area (not run during the workshop).





Some of the covariates: bedrock model ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr, geological age and distance to the coast








The full list of global covariates






Compared with the global script, a few global layers are not in the South Africa set (Bouguer anomaly, permafrost, mean annual temperature and the other WorldClim variables except wind). Permafrost is irrelevant in South Africa anyway!

title: 2. Covariates
text:
Step 2.8: Neighbourhood geology (NEW)
The bedrock ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr model (r.srsrq1) and the age of the geological units (r.meanage_geol) describe the rock directly under each 1 km pixel, with sharp boundaries between units. But bioavailable Sr at a site does not come only from the rock under it:

soils form on sediments, colluvium and alluvium transported from the surrounding hills;
dust and runoff mix material from the surrounding area;
plants and animals integrate Sr over their root zone or home range;
the sample coordinates and the geological contacts both have location errors of hundreds of metres to kilometres.

To represent this, we compute the mean of the bedrock ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr and of the geological age within circles of 5, 10 and 25 km around each pixel (a moving-window or “focal” mean). The random forest can then learn at which scale the geology best predicts bioavailable ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr.

focal_dir <- "Project_Raster/neighbourhood"
dir.create(focal_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

focal_names <- c()
for (v in c("r.srsrq1", "r.meanage_geol")) {
  for (km in c(5, 10, 25)) {
    name <- sprintf("%s.f%02d", v, km)               # e.g. r.srsrq1.f05 = mean within 5 km
    file <- file.path(focal_dir, paste0(name, ".tif"))
    if (!file.exists(file)) {
      r <- get(v)
      w <- focalMat(r, km * 1000, type = "circle")   # circular window, radius in metres
      w[w > 0] <- 1                                   # simple (unweighted) mean
      f <- focal(r, w = w, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE)
      f <- mask(f, r)                                 # keep the land mask of the original raster
      writeRaster(f, file, overwrite = TRUE)
    }
    assign(name, terra::rast(file))
    focal_names <- c(focal_names, name)
  }
}
focal_names
plot(c(r.srsrq1, r.srsrq1.f05, r.srsrq1.f10, r.srsrq1.f25), nc = 4)




Output of Step 2.8: bedrock ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr at the pixel scale and averaged within 5, 10 and 25 km








Why stop at 25 km?



In the training data, adding these six layers improves the spatial cross-validation R² from ~0.5 to ~0.7. Going beyond 25 km does not help: at 50 km the layers become so smooth that they behave like coordinates.

title: 3. Regression matrix
text:
In this section




You’ll learn: how to build a clean regression matrix, and what correlated covariates do to a random forest
You’ll need: sr_proj (Section 1) and stack_all (Section 2)
Time: about 30 minutes

title: 3. Regression matrix
text:
Overview
We now have a training set (sites with ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr in Eckert IV) and covariates in the same projection. We overlay the sites on the maps, extract the value of every covariate under each site, and assemble everything into one regression matrix: one row per site, one column per covariate.

title: 3. Regression matrix
text:
Step 3.1: Extract






Sites on a nodata pixel



Some sites fall on a pixel with no value, often around coastlines, rivers and lakes. To avoid losing them, the function below takes the value of the nearest non-NA pixel within 5 km.




Show the extraction function
# Extract the values of all layers under the points; for points falling on a NA
# pixel, take the nearest non-NA pixel within max_dist (in map units, here metres)
extract_nearest_non_na <- function(points, r, max_dist = 5000) {
  v <- terra::extract(r, vect(points), ID = FALSE)
  xy <- st_coordinates(points)
  for (i in which(!complete.cases(v))) {
    # small window of rasters around the point
    rr <- crop(r, ext(xy[i, 1] - max_dist, xy[i, 1] + max_dist, xy[i, 2] - max_dist, xy[i, 2] + max_dist))
    vals <- values(rr)
    cxy <- xyFromCell(rr, 1:ncell(rr))
    d <- sqrt((cxy[, 1] - xy[i, 1])^2 + (cxy[, 2] - xy[i, 2])^2)
    # for each layer with a NA, take the value of the nearest non-NA pixel
    for (j in which(is.na(v[i, ]))) {
      ok <- !is.na(vals[, j])
      if (any(ok)) v[i, j] <- vals[ok, j][which.min(d[ok])]
    }
  }
  v
}



# For each covariate extract values under points (all covariates at once)
s_proj <- sr_proj
extracted <- extract_nearest_non_na(s_proj, stack_all)

# Number of points that still have NA (no valid pixel within 5 km)
sum(!complete.cases(extracted))

s_xy <- data.frame(st_coordinates(s_proj))

                        Longitude = s_proj$collection_decimal_longitude,

title: 3. Regression matrix
text:
Step 3.4: Clean the regression matrix

Remove NA rows. There shouldn’t be many, thanks to the nearest-pixel extraction.
Handle outliers. Random forest predictions are not sensitive to outliers, but performance metrics can be. As in the global dataset, we remove values > 0.8.
One value per site. Several samples at the same site are not independent, so we aggregate them with the median.


# remove NA values cases if any from the dataset
sr_proj_xy <- sr_proj_xy[!is.na(sr_proj_xy$r.srsrq1),]

# Optional. Filter 'sr_proj_xy' to exclude rows with super high or zero values
sr_proj_xy1 <- sr_proj_xy[sr_proj_xy$X87Sr86Sr <= 0.8, ]
sr_proj_xy2 <- sr_proj_xy1[!(sr_proj_xy1$X87Sr86Sr == 0), ]

#Aggregate all samples by latitude and longitude to avoid having multiple samples per site
#(the categorical maps, r.geomap and r.vegmap, are aggregated with the median too; this is fine
# because all samples of one site fall in the same class)
sr_agg1 <- aggregate(sr_proj_xy2, by = list(sr_proj_xy2$Latitude, sr_proj_xy2$Longitude), FUN = median, na.rm = TRUE)
sr_agg1 <- sr_agg1[,3:ncol(sr_agg1)]   # remove the two grouping columns added by aggregate()
nrow(sr_agg1)

title: 3. Regression matrix
text:
Step 3.5: Choose the candidate covariates
Before any statistics, think about the processes! Three groups of covariates need care in South Africa:

Coarse atmospheric deposition layers (r.dust, r.salt, r.volc, r.fire, r.foss, r.biofuels, r.biogenic). Inside South Africa they are smooth gradients that the random forest can use as a proxy for latitude and longitude: the model “memorises” where the samples are. Random cross-validation looks good, but the model does not transfer to regions without data (see Section 4). Sea-salt input is better captured here by distance to the coast (r.distance).
Categorical maps with hundreds of classes (r.geomap, r.vegmap). Most classes contain no training site, and the model cannot say anything about a class it has never seen. Their information is largely carried by the continuous geology layers.
Duplicated layers: r.m1 is identical to r.srsrq1 in this clipped set.


candidate_set <- "all"    # "no_coarse" or "all"

coarse_layers      <- c("r.dust", "r.salt", "r.volc", "r.fire", "r.foss", "r.biofuels", "r.biogenic")
categorical_layers <- c("r.geomap", "r.vegmap")

drop_layers <- c("r.m1", categorical_layers)
if (candidate_set == "no_coarse") drop_layers <- c(drop_layers, coarse_layers)

candidates <- setdiff(predictor_names, drop_layers)
length(candidates)







🧩 Your turn (later)



Run the whole script with candidate_set <- "all" and with "no_coarse". Compare the random and spatial cross-validation (Step 4.5) and the shape of the patterns in the maps.

title: 3. Regression matrix
section: Step 3.6: Check for highly correlated covariates
text:
Step 3.6: Check for highly correlated covariates
Random forest can handle collinear variables to some extent, but strong collinearity complicates the interpretation. Before VSURF, we remove one variable of every pair with |r| > 0.9: findCorrelation() (caret) removes the variable with the largest mean correlation with all the others.

#check correlation between covariates and remove redundant variables
cor_mat <- cor(sr_agg1[, candidates], use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
corrplot(cor_mat, method = "color", type = "upper", tl.cex = 0.5, tl.col = "black")

high_cor <- findCorrelation(cor_mat, cutoff = 0.9, names = TRUE)
high_cor   # variables removed because R > 0.9 with another variable

kept <- setdiff(candidates, high_cor)

sr_agg <- sr_agg1[, c("X87Sr86Sr", "X", "Y", kept)]
# Remove incomplete cases with NA in covariates
sr_agg <- sr_agg[complete.cases(sr_agg),]
# Save table on directory
write.table(sr_agg,"Output/sr_agg_all.txt",sep = "\t",col.names = T, row.names = F, quote = F)

Think · Pair · Share: correlated covariates
Many covariates carry the same information: bedrock Sr at 1, 5, 10 and 25 km; rainfall, aridity and PET; Ca at 0–20 and 20–50 cm… What does collinearity do to a random forest, and how do we deal with it?


💭 Think 2 min

Why are they correlated: the same process, the same source dataset, or a shared spatial gradient?



🤝 Pair 3 min

high_cor

With your neighbour:

What does collinearity change in a random forest: the predictions? variable importance? partial dependence?
Which variables were removed? Would you have removed the same ones?



📣 Share 3 min
Tell the room:

What strategies remove or handle collinearity?
What does this script do, and what would you do differently?










Things you might have noticed





🔗 The strongest pairs in our data

Same source dataset: r.meanage_geol / r.minage_geol / r.maxage_geol (r = 1.00); r.africa.Ca.0 / r.africa.Ca.20 (1.00) and the other iSDA depth pairs (0.97–1.00); r.fire / r.biofuels / r.biogenic (0.99), all from the same aerosol model.
Same process at different scales: r.srsrq1.f05 / r.srsrq1.f10 (0.96), r.srsrq1.f10 / r.srsrq1.f25 (0.92).
Shared climate gradient: r.map / r.ai (0.95), r.map / r.ph (−0.91), since wetter soils are more leached and acidic.

🌲 What collinearity does to a random forest

Predictions: little effect. Each split simply uses whichever correlated variable is drawn (mtry).
Importance: shared or diluted between “twins”. A key process can look unimportant because its twin substitutes for it.
Interpretation: partial dependence plots average over impossible combinations (e.g. high 5 km Sr with low 25 km Sr).
Selection is unstable: which twin survives can change with the random seed.

🛠️ What the script does

findCorrelation(): for each pair with |r| > 0.9, drop the variable with the highest mean correlation: 64 → 42 candidates.
VSURF (Step 4.3): the thresholding step removes noise; the prediction step removes redundancy.
Spatial pruning (Step 4.4): drop variables that worsen the spatial-CV RMSE by > 2%.

💡 Other strategies

Choose by process and resolution: keep the twin with the clearest mechanism.
A lower threshold (0.7–0.8), or variance inflation factors (VIF).
Combine a group into one axis (PCA, composite index), at the cost of interpretability.
Conditional or grouped permutation importance (Strobl et al. 2008).
Remember: correlation among the training sites ≠ correlation across the whole map.

Take-home: collinearity rarely hurts random forest predictions, but it blurs which process the model has actually learned.

Key takeaways




The regression matrix has one row per site (median of all samples at that site) and one column per covariate.

title: 5. Interpreting the model
text:
In this section




You’ll learn: how to read variable importance and partial dependence plots, and check them against what we know of strontium isotopes
You’ll need: RF_all and training_rf (Section 4)
Time: about 15 minutes

title: 5. Interpreting the model
text:
Overview
A random forest averages hundreds of trees, which makes it accurate but hard to interpret. Two tools help us look inside:

Variable importance: how much the predictions get worse when the values of one covariate are shuffled (permutation importance).
Partial dependence plots (PDPs): how the predicted ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr changes as one covariate varies, averaged over all the others.

User knowledge of Sr cycling is crucial here: the model only finds patterns, it is up to us to decide whether they make sense.

title: 5. Interpreting the model
text:
Step 4.8a: Variable importance


Show the code
# Compute the variable importance using caret
var_imp <- varImp(RF_all, scale = TRUE)

# Convert the results into a data frame
imp_df <- as.data.frame(var_imp$importance)

# Create the importance plot
imp <- ggplot(imp_df, aes(x = reorder(rownames(imp_df), Overall), y = Overall)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "lightblue", color = "black") +
  coord_flip() +  # Flip the axes for better readability
  labs(x = "Predictor Variables", y = "Importance", title = "Variable Importance Plot") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 12),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 14),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10))
imp
ggsave("Output/FigS3.pdf", imp, width = 14, height = 12)





Output of Step 4.8 (Fig. S3): permutation importance of the 16 predictors in the final model


r.srsrq1.f25, the mean bedrock ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr within 25 km, is by far the most important predictor, followed by r.srsrq1.f05, r.meanage_geol, r.africa.Ca.0, r.wetland and r.distance. Notice that the pixel-scale bedrock model r.srsrq1 comes last: its neighbourhood versions carry the same information.






Importance is not a process



Importance tells us which covariates the model uses, not why. Correlated covariates share their importance (Section 3), and a covariate can be important because it acts as a proxy for location.

title: 5. Interpreting the model

Step 4.8b: Partial dependence plots
Each panel shows the predicted ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr as one covariate varies while the others are averaged out. The histogram below each curve shows where the training sites are.


Show the code
# List of predictors to plot
predictors <- vars_final

# Generate partial dependence data for all predictors
# (grid.resolution = 25 points per variable: fast and smooth enough)
partial_data_list <- lapply(predictors, function(predictor) {
  pdp::partial(RF_all$finalModel, pred.var = predictor, train = training_rf[, predictors], grid.resolution = 25)
})

# Name each list element by the predictor variable
names(partial_data_list) <- predictors

# Common y-axis range for all the PDPs (adapted automatically to the data)
pdp_range <- range(unlist(lapply(partial_data_list, function(d) d$yhat)))

# Create ggplot for each partial dependence plot (PDP) and histogram
plots <- lapply(names(partial_data_list), function(predictor) {
  partial_data <- partial_data_list[[predictor]]

  # Extract data for the predictor variable (for histogram)
x_data <- training_rf[[predictor]]

  # Create the PDP plot (Partial Dependence Plot)
pdp_plot <- ggplot() +
    geom_line(data = partial_data, aes(x = .data[[predictor]], y = .data[["yhat"]]), color = "blue", linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_point(data = partial_data, aes(x = .data[[predictor]], y = .data[["yhat"]]), color = "blue", size = 2) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = range(x_data), ylim = pdp_range) +  # Same y-axis range for all predictors
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Predicted Value") +             # Remove x-axis title
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      axis.text = element_text(size = 8),               # Smaller axis numbers
      axis.title = element_text(size = 10),             # Smaller axis titles
      plot.title = element_blank(),
      panel.grid = element_blank(),
      axis.text.x = element_blank(),                    # Remove x-axis numbers
      axis.title.x = element_blank(),                   # Remove x-axis title
      axis.ticks.x = element_blank()
    )

  # Create the Histogram for the predictor distribution
hist_plot <- ggplot() +
    geom_histogram(data = data.frame(x = x_data), aes(x = x, y = after_stat(density)),
                   bins = 30, fill = "lightblue", color = "darkblue", alpha = 0.5) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = range(x_data)) +  # Align x-axis with the PDP
    labs(x = predictor, y = "Density") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      axis.text = element_text(size = 8),           # Smaller axis numbers
      axis.title = element_text(size = 10),         # Smaller axis titles
      plot.title = element_blank(),
      panel.grid = element_blank(),
      axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8),         # Smaller x-axis numbers
      axis.ticks.x = element_blank()
    )

  # Return the combined plot as a list (PDP + histogram)
  list(pdp_plot = pdp_plot, hist_plot = hist_plot)
})

# Combine both plots (PDP and histogram) into a single plot with aligned x-axes
combined_plots <- lapply(plots, function(p) {
  p$pdp_plot + p$hist_plot + plot_layout(ncol = 1, heights = c(2, 1))
})

# Combine all plots into a single layout (adjust ncol to 3 or any number for better arrangement)
final_plot <- wrap_plots(combined_plots, ncol = 4)
final_plot
# Save the final plot as a PDF
ggsave("Output/FigS4.pdf", final_plot, width = 16, height = 14)

Think · Pair · Share: reading partial dependence
Each curve is the predicted ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr as one covariate varies, averaged over all the others. Does each relationship make sense with what we know of strontium isotopes?


💭 Think 2 min
On your own, describe the curves (start with the six most important predictors):

Rising, falling, flat, or a step?
Where along the x-axis are the data?



🤝 Pair 3 min
With your neighbour:

Match each curve to a Sr process: rock age and Rb/Sr, sea-salt input, carbonate and exchangeable Ca, mixing.
Which curves surprise you? Does r.africa.Ca.0 go the way you expected? And r.wetland?



📣 Share 3 min
Tell the room:

Which curve would you trust least, and why?
Can a strange curve point to a problem with the data, a covariate or the model?










Things you might have noticed





✔️ Consistent with Sr cycling

Neighbourhood bedrock Sr (f25, f05): bioavailable Sr rises with the bedrock model, but the slope is well below 1:1. Atmospheric Sr and the preferential weathering of low-⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr minerals pull the values together.
Geological age: older units are more radiogenic (⁸⁷Rb decay), in steps.
Distance to coast: lowest within ~75 km of the sea, then a plateau. Sea-salt Sr (0.7092) dilutes the rock signal.

❓ Worth discussing

The sharp step in f25 at ~0.718–0.720: a real threshold, or a few radiogenic sites (sparse rug) driving one split?
Extractable Ca: a weak positive effect. Did you expect high Ca → carbonate → lower ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr? Could Ca instead track arid, calcrete-rich soils over old basement?
Wetland: higher Sr where wetland cover is low. A process, or a proxy for location?
r.srsrq1 (bedrock under the pixel) has ~0 importance, while its 5 and 25 km versions dominate. What does that say about where bioavailable Sr comes from?
The coarse layers (r.salt, r.dust, r.volc, r.foss) have flat curves and low importance. Process, or proxy for location?

⚠️ Read PDPs carefully

Flat ends beyond the data: random forest cannot extrapolate, so predictions stay constant outside the training range.
Correlated covariates (f05, f25): the curve averages over unrealistic combinations.
Amplitude ≠ importance, and interactions are hidden: try ICE curves or 2-D PDPs.

Take-home: a PDP tests the model against your knowledge of Sr cycling. It does not prove a process.

Summary






Key takeaways




Neighbourhood bedrock ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr dominates the model, followed by geological age, soil Ca, wetland and distance to the coast.
Most partial dependence curves agree with Sr cycling; the ones that don’t are worth a closer look.
Random forests cannot extrapolate beyond the range of the training data.
